reference.source: Oxford Handbook of Oncology / Infectious Diseases Society of America neutropenia guidance
clinicalPearls: A necrotising inflammation of the caecum and right colon (typhlitis) occurring in profound neutropenia, classically after intensive chemotherapy for acute leukaemia and in the post-transplant setting.
The characteristic clinical triad is fever, right iliac fossa pain and neutropenia, often with watery or bloody diarrhoea, nausea and abdominal distension.

CT of the abdomen is the imaging modality of choice, showing circumferential bowel-wall thickening (typically greater than four millimetres), caecal distension, pericolic fat stranding and, in severe disease, pneumatosis intestinalis.
Colonoscopy and contrast enema should be avoided because of the high risk of perforation in inflamed, friable, neutropenic bowel.

Management is predominantly conservative: bowel rest, nasogastric decompression if obstructed, intravenous fluids, and broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Gram-negative organisms and anaerobes, with antifungal cover added for persistent fever.
Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor and correction of thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy support recovery, which closely tracks neutrophil count recovery.
Surgery is reserved for defined indications: free perforation, uncontrolled gastrointestinal haemorrhage, persistent obstruction, or clinical deterioration despite maximal medical therapy.

Distinguish from Clostridioides difficile colitis and acute appendicitis, and continue treatment until both symptoms resolve and neutropenia recovers, as relapse can occur with subsequent chemotherapy cycles.
reference.pathophysiology: Chemotherapy-induced mucosal injury combines with profound neutropenia to breach the bowel's defences, most severely in the caecum, whose distensibility and relatively poor blood supply predispose it to injury. Loss of mucosal integrity allows intramural invasion by gut flora—Gram-negative bacilli, anaerobes and fungi such as Candida—producing oedema, transmural inflammation, haemorrhage and necrosis. The absence of an effective neutrophil response permits unchecked bacterial proliferation and translocation, driving bacteraemia and sepsis; progressive wall necrosis may culminate in pneumatosis and perforation.
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count confirming neutropenia and assessing platelets
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis
Stool for Clostridioides difficile toxin and enteric pathogens
Serum lactate and venous blood gas
Serial abdominal examination with erect and supine abdominal radiographs if perforation is suspected
redFlags: Peritonitis or radiological free intraperitoneal air
Rising lactate or persistent deterioration despite therapy
reference.prognosis: Outcome is closely tied to neutrophil recovery; with prompt supportive care and antimicrobials many patients recover fully. Perforation, uncontrolled haemorrhage or full-thickness necrosis markedly worsen prognosis and carry a high mortality.
pitfalls: Performing colonoscopy or contrast enema and precipitating perforation
Delaying broad-spectrum antibiotics while awaiting imaging or cultures
Operating for presumed appendicitis when conservative management is appropriate
Failing to add antifungal cover for persistent fever
Stopping treatment once the patient is afebrile while still neutropenic
references: Infectious Diseases Society of America guideline on the management of neutropenic fever
management: Manage conservatively with bowel rest, nasogastric decompression if obstructed and intravenous fluid resuscitation
Start broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Gram-negative bacilli and anaerobes, adding antifungal cover such as an echinocandin or azole for persistent fever
Support neutrophil recovery with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, since outcome tracks the returning neutrophil count
Correct thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy with blood-product support
Avoid colonoscopy and contrast enema because of the high perforation risk in friable neutropenic bowel
Monitor with serial examination, abdominal imaging and lactate for perforation, uncontrolled haemorrhage or transmural necrosis
Involve surgery for operative intervention if perforation, full-thickness necrosis or uncontrolled bleeding develops
Coordinate haematology and oncology care, including review and timing of the causative chemotherapy regimen
